title: ILCA 6

overview.heading: ILCA 6 dinghy
overview.text: A fast boat for one sailor, designed by Bruce Kirby in 1970 and now raced all over the world and at the Olympic Games. The ILCA 6 rig, formerly called the Laser Radial, has a shorter lower mast and a smaller sail than the ILCA 7, so it suits lighter and younger sailors. Every boat is built to the same strict rules, so races are won by the sailor, not the boat.
overview.hint: Click any part of the boat or pick one from the list. Drag to look around, scroll or pinch to zoom. Move the boom slider to change course against the wind, and watch the mast bend.

hull.name: Hull
hull.text: The body of the boat, made of fibreglass. The bottom is a shallow V at the front and almost flat at the back, with soft rounded edges. In a strong wind the flat back half lifts the boat up to skim over the water. This is called planing.

deck.name: Deck
deck.text: The top of the hull. The ILCA is a decked boat: waves that come on board run off again, and the closed hull is full of air, so it floats high even after a capsize. You sit on the side deck to sail.
deck.note: The hull and the deck are two mouldings glued together at the rounded edge. Press Explode to lift the deck off.

cockpit.name: Cockpit
cockpit.text: The small open well where your feet go. Its floor is above the water outside, so water drains away by itself through the bailer.

transom.name: Transom
transom.text: The flat back of the hull. The rudder hangs on two fittings here, and the drain bung is in its top corner.

mastStep.name: Mast step
mastStep.text: A tube moulded through the foredeck down to the bottom of the hull. The mast simply drops into it. No wires hold an ILCA mast up.

daggerboardTrunk.name: Daggerboard slot
daggerboardTrunk.text: The slot in the sloping well in front of the cockpit. The daggerboard slides down through it and out of the bottom of the hull. A rubber brake at the back of the slot holds the board where you put it.
daggerboardTrunk.note: The class rules call the daggerboard the centreboard.

bowEye.name: Bow eye
bowEye.text: A strong steel eye on the foredeck. Use it to tow the boat or tie it up. The daggerboard's shock cord is fixed here, and the hull number is moulded under it.

gudgeons.name: Rudder fittings
gudgeons.text: Two gudgeons (eyes) on the transom. The pins (pintles) on the rudder head drop into them, so the rudder can swing from side to side.

drainBung.name: Drain bung
drainBung.text: A plug in the transom. Take it out after sailing so that water inside the hull can drain away. Put it back before you launch!

selfBailer.name: Self-bailer
selfBailer.text: A small flap in the cockpit floor. Open it when the boat is going fast and it sucks the water out of the cockpit. Close it when you go slowly, or water comes in.

hikingStrap.name: Hiking strap
hikingStrap.text: The padded strap along the middle of the cockpit. Hook your feet under it and lean out over the side to keep the boat flat in a breeze. This is called hiking.

travellerFairleads.name: Traveller fairleads
travellerFairleads.text: Two plastic eyes at the back corners of the deck, and a clam cleat between them. The traveller rope runs through the eyes and is locked in the cleat.

deckBlock.name: Deck blocks
deckBlock.text: A fitting just behind the mast with two small blocks. They turn the cunningham and the outhaul from the mast back toward you, so you can adjust them while you sail.

controlCleats.name: Control cleats
controlCleats.text: Two cam cleats in front of the cockpit: the cunningham on the port side, the outhaul on the starboard side. Pull a rope and it locks; flick it up and it runs free.

plaque.name: Building plaque
plaque.text: A small metal plate on the back wall of the cockpit. It shows the boat's official number, so every ILCA can be identified.

mastLower.name: Lower mast
mastLower.text: The bottom section of the mast. The ILCA 6 lower is shorter, thinner and bendier than the ILCA 7 one. Change only this part and the sail, and you have a different rig.

mastTop.name: Top mast
mastTop.text: The top section is the same for every ILCA rig. It slides 305 mm into the lower section until its collar rests on top. Move the boom slider: the mast bends back most when you sail toward the wind.

gooseneck.name: Gooseneck
gooseneck.text: The fitting that joins the boom to the mast. A bolt holds the front of the boom, and a small block on it leads the outhaul down to the deck.

boom.name: Boom
boom.text: The pole along the bottom of the sail. It swings across every time you tack or gybe, and it is low on an ILCA, so keep your head down!

windIndicator.name: Wind indicator
windIndicator.text: A small vane on a stick at the front of the mast. It points into the wind. Move the boom slider and watch it turn as the wind direction changes.

sail.name: Sail
sail.text: A triangular sail of 5.76 m². It has no halyard: its front edge is a sleeve that you slide over the mast before you put the mast in the boat. The ILCA 6 sail is made of panels that fan out from the corners.

luffSleeve.name: Luff sleeve
luffSleeve.text: The front edge of the sail is a long tube of sailcloth. It slides down over the mast like a sock, so the mast and the sail work together as one curved wing.

luff.name: Luff
luff.text: The front edge of the sail, held by the mast inside the sleeve. Pull the cunningham to tighten it and flatten the sail in strong wind.

leech.name: Leech
leech.text: The back edge of the sail. It curves out a little, and three battens help it keep that shape.

foot.name: Foot
foot.text: The bottom edge of the sail. It is held only at its two corners (a loose foot), so it can curve out to the side of the boom.

head.name: Head
head.text: The top corner of the sail, at the very top of the mast.

tack.name: Tack
tack.text: The bottom front corner of the sail, just above the gooseneck. The cunningham pulls the sail down near here.

clew.name: Clew
clew.text: The bottom back corner of the sail. The outhaul pulls it toward the end of the boom, and a strap holds it down on the boom.

battens.name: Battens
battens.text: Three flat strips in pockets on the leech: two long ones and a short one at the top. They stop the back edge of the sail from curling and flapping.
spec: At ¼, ½ and ¾ of the leech

window.name: Window
window.text: A clear panel low in the sail. Look through it for boats hidden behind your sail. No stickers or adverts may cover it.

sailNumber.name: Sail number
sailNumber.text: The country letters (BUL is Bulgaria) and the boat's number. They slope like the battens. The starboard side is printed higher than the port side, so the two sides never cover each other.
sailNumber.note: This boat is BUL 2026. The class logo is a trademark, so it is left off this model.

telltales.name: Telltales
telltales.text: Short strips of wool or ribbon on the sail: red on the port side, green on the starboard side. When they all stream back smoothly, your sail is set well.

daggerboard.name: Daggerboard
daggerboard.text: The flat foil you push down through the slot. Under water it stops the boat sliding sideways, so you can sail across the wind and toward it. Pull it partly up when the wind is behind you.
daggerboard.note: The stopper at the top stops it dropping through the slot. The orange loops are the handle.

rudder.name: Rudder blade
rudder.text: The blade at the back that steers the boat. It turns on a bolt in the rudder head: in shallow water you can lift it, then pull it down again with the downhaul.

rudderHead.name: Rudder head
rudderHead.text: The aluminium box that holds the rudder blade. Its pins hang on the transom fittings, and the tiller slots into its top.

tiller.name: Tiller
tiller.text: The stick fixed to the rudder head. Push it away from you and the boat turns toward the wind. Pull it toward you and the boat turns away. It runs under the traveller rope.

tillerExtension.name: Tiller extension
tillerExtension.text: A long stick joined to the tiller by a flexible joint, so you can steer while you hike out. Most sailors hold it across the body, like a microphone.

mainsheet.name: Mainsheet
mainsheet.text: The rope that pulls the boom in and lets it out. It runs from the end of the boom, round the traveller block, along the boom and down to the block in the cockpit, where you hold it.

ratchetBlock.name: Mainsheet block
ratchetBlock.text: The pulley on a spring at the front of the cockpit. Its ratchet lets the mainsheet run out easily but grips it while you hold it, so your hand gets less tired.

boomBlocks.name: Boom blocks
boomBlocks.text: Two blocks under the boom with a steel strap between them. They guide the mainsheet along the boom.
spec: 71 mm from the end of the boom

traveller.name: Traveller
traveller.text: A rope across the back of the boat with a block riding on it. The mainsheet runs round the block, which slides to the side as the boom goes out. Pull the traveller tight to bring the boom close to the corner of the boat when you sail upwind.

vang.name: Vang (kicker)
vang.text: Blocks and rope between the bottom of the mast and the boom. The vang pulls the boom down, which bends the mast and flattens the sail. Use more of it in strong wind.

cunningham.name: Cunningham
cunningham.text: A rope that pulls the front of the sail down through an eye near the tack. Pull it hard in strong wind to flatten the sail. Let it off in light wind.

outhaul.name: Outhaul
outhaul.text: A rope that pulls the clew toward the end of the boom. Tight makes the bottom of the sail flatter for strong wind. Looser makes it fuller for light wind and waves.

clewTieDown.name: Clew strap
clewTieDown.text: A strap round the boom and through the clew. It keeps the back corner of the sail close to the boom while the outhaul slides it back and forth.

hikingStrapSupport.name: Hiking strap line
hikingStrapSupport.text: A short line from the back of the hiking strap to two eyes on the cockpit wall, and a shock cord that lifts the strap. Set the line so the strap sits at the right height for your legs.

daggerboardRetainer.name: Daggerboard shock cord
daggerboardRetainer.text: A shock cord from the top of the daggerboard to the bow eye. It keeps the board with the boat if you capsize, and it holds the board at the height you choose.

rudderDownhaul.name: Rudder downhaul
rudderDownhaul.text: A thin line that pulls the rudder blade fully down and locks in a cleat on the tiller. Keep the blade down while you race.

mastRetainer.name: Mast retaining line
mastRetainer.text: A short line between the bottom of the mast and the deck fitting. If the boat turns upside down, it stops the mast sliding out of its tube. The class rules require it.

compass.name: Compass
compass.text: Optional. It may be fixed to the deck or the cockpit, but only with screws that do not go into the hull. Racers use it to notice when the wind changes direction.
